papers.title: 具身智能动作决策的最小证据边界 / Minimal Evidence Boundaries for Action Decisions in Embodied Agents
papers.authors: YANGZHOU
papers.abstract: 本稿为中文方法与理论研究草稿,提出以当前动作是否可被证据确认,作为进一步获取观测的停止条件。稿件区分静态离线最短证书与在线自适应查询代价,并给出基本推导、动态失效反例与后续比较实验方案。研究仍处于探索阶段,新颖性与实际工程收益尚未建立;本文不是经同行评审的期刊论文。 Minimal Evidence Boundaries for Action Decisions in Embodied Agents. This Chinese-language methods and theory draft studies action-specific evidence acquisition, distinguishing offline certificates from online adaptive query costs. It includes elementary propositions, a dynamic invalidation counterexample, and a falsifiable evaluation plan. Novelty and practical benefits remain to be established. This is an exploratory preprint, not a peer-reviewed journal article. Validation is limited to a four-bit static logical model: 16 worlds, 81 partial-evidence states and 256 compatible world/evidence pairs. The included standard-library Python program and actual JSON output reproduce these checks. There are no physical robot experiments, learned-model benchmarks or claims of real-world safety. Query-count comparisons apply only to the stated toy model and uniform distribution. Files: six-page Chinese manuscript PDF, editable DOCX, Python checker, actual enumeration results and reproduction instructions. Manuscript version completed on 2026-11-13; repository publication date is 2026-11-14. The manuscript's statement that it had not yet been submitted describes its status when written. AI assistance was used for ideation, literature discovery, drafting, formalization, coding and typesetting. Related work and limitations are explicitly discussed. The listed author and affiliation follow author-provided information: YANGZHOU, 梗必爆具身交互AI研究院 (Genbibao Embodied AI Research Institute), ORCID 0009-0005-4736-2097. papers.title: Whole-Body Contact-Rich Compliant Motion Planning Based on Morphology Representation
papers.authors: Chengjin Wang, Zheng Yan, Yanmin Zhou, Runjie Shen, Bin He
papers.abstract: Robots operating in cluttered environments require whole-body contact-rich motion planning to safely interact with surrounding objects. However, model-based methods struggle with unknown interaction dynamics, while learning-based methods often depend on task-specific demonstrations or rewards. This paper proposes a physics-model-guided motion planning framework that learns task-agnostic whole-body interactions through material-point morphology representation and interaction prediction supervision. The representation encodes distributed body motion and tactile states with consistent body correspondence, accommodating time-varying contact configurations. A tactile-driven interaction planner generates physically informed motion references to supervise MorphoPlanner, an end-to-end network that predicts future whole-body motion morphologies from task goals and current interaction states without task-specific demonstrations or reward design. A dataset of 749 K tactile interaction samples is constructed for training and evaluation. Simulation and real-world dual-arm experiments demonstrate compliant interactions and improved planning performance over representative baselines, achieving 95.5–100% success rates in dense cluttered scenarios. These results demonstrate the potential of morphology-based physical supervision for whole-body interaction planning in unknown environments.

papers.title: Who Is the Agent Talking To? Participant-Aware Role Switching for Embodied Student-Support Dialogue
papers.authors: Iro Samuel, Filip Janik, Ewa Olton, Robert Smales, Harris Spratt, Shea Tait, Md Zia Ullah, Yanchao Yu
papers.abstract: We present RPO-PDT, an embodied conversational agent that adapts its conversational role to the current participant. It acts as a Personal Development Tutor (PDT) when supporting students and as a simulated student when faculty rehearse tutoring strategies. Voluntary closed-set participant verification informs a confidence-controlled role manager: stable enrolled-faculty matches activate the Student role, while enrolled students and unmatched participants use the default PDT role and uncertain observations cause no transition. The system combines Furhat interaction, Rasa orchestration, institutional retrieval, safeguarding, and LLM-based generation. User control is preserved through manual role override, consent-based facial enrolment, temporary interaction identifiers, and explicit retention or deletion of enrolled profiles. The demonstration exposes both role-switching behaviour and these privacy controls in interaction.

papers.title: When Will You Hand It Over? A Hidden Start Delay Makes Self-Play Handover Robust to Unfamiliar Partners
papers.authors: Mohammad Khoshnazar, Mike Degany, Deyuan Qu, Qing Yang, Matyas Szanto
papers.abstract: Cooperative self-play can teach a humanoid to receive an object without any human data, but the partner it meets after training is never the one it trained with; we show that a fluent self-play handover policy breaks with unfamiliar partners, identify the main cause, and repair it. In a physics-based parcel handover between a Unitree G1 and a learned giver, both trained by alternating PPO self-play, the receiver completes 95% and 90% of handovers with its own partner (two training seeds) but only 31% with scripted partners it has never met. Paired interventions isolate the cause: under a shared reward the learned giver always starts its offer at once, so the receiver learns a single rendezvous, and delaying its own partner by one second cuts success from 95% to 6% (87% to 34% in the second seed). We introduce hidden start-delay randomisation (HSD), a one-line rule on the learned partner that the receiver never observes. After 300 further updates, success with unseen scripted partners rises from 31% to 80% in both seeds, against 35--41% for a budget-matched control. The gain holds on a fresh scenario seed, on eleven held-out partner conditions and on partners that start later than any training delay; it cuts high-force contact three- to five-fold and needs no retraining of the partner.

papers.title: When Does Cross-View Consistency Matter in Multi-View Appearance Augmentation? A Controlled Study for Visuomotor Policies
papers.authors: Zixuan Jiang
papers.abstract: Multi-view visual augmentation often seeks consistency across cameras, but it is unclear which forms of consistency matter for downstream control. We use simulation-state replay to manipulate cross-view coupling while preserving the per-camera perturbation distributions, physical trajectories, and action labels. Across seven LIBERO manipulation tasks, marginal-matched changes in global appearance, ghost injection, and target color have small average costs for a late-fusion Diffusion Policy: point estimates are near zero or negative, and the largest upper endpoint of the 90% posterior credible intervals is 2.55 percentage points. In contrast, geometrically anti-coupled observations reduce success by 3.30 percentage points relative to coupled observations (90% CrI [0.64, 6.28]), with displacement magnitude, direction marginals, and the number of affected views matched. Camera interventions reveal substantial dependence on wrist-view geometry, while feature analysis shows appearance sensitivity patterns associated with the factors randomized during training. ACT shows a higher target-color cost estimate than DP, with uncertainty that includes zero and sensitivity to task composition. Within the tested tasks and policy configurations, these findings motivate selective consistency constraints: appearance coupling can sometimes be relaxed, whereas task-relevant geometry and cross-view spatial correspondence warrant protection.

papers.title: When Cooperation Must Change: Semantic Strategy Unlearning in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Wenhan Wu, Linghan Chen, Yudong Gao, Fan Yang, Honglong Chen, Kai Yin, Jiawei Jiang, Chuang Hu
papers.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) supports coordinated decision-making in distributed Web services, multi-robot control, and collaborative games through learned coordination conventions. When deployment requirements change, a previously useful convention may become obsolete or unsafe. For example, revised cache-sharing permissions in Web content delivery may require caches to abandon a learned division of storage and serving roles while maintaining efficient delivery. Teams must therefore remove the specified convention while preserving useful cooperation. This is challenging because the same relational pattern can be reproduced by different agents across different histories. Runtime shielding leaves the underlying coordination preference intact and can impair task progress, while existing reinforcement unlearning and trajectory-deletion methods do not directly target role-invariant conventions. This paper formalizes this problem as semantic coordination-strategy unlearning and proposes CARVE.CARVE uses causal coordination attribution to identify influential interactions and retain-aware subspace updates to limit interference with unrelated behaviors. Counterfactual re-coordination helps agents learn productive alternatives, while adversarial auditing tests whether the target convention can still be recovered. Accepted updates are merged into decentralized actors for direct deployment. Evaluation across five cooperative MARL benchmarks shows that CARVE reduces mean nominal convention-completion and worst-case elicitation rates by 91.4\% and 83.3\%, respectively.The median utility loss is 5.9\%, and measured inference latency matches that of the original policies.

papers.title: WeatherDreamer: Learning a World Model from Multimodal Earth Observations
papers.authors: Kate Duffy, Elise Penn, Tristan Ballard, August Posch, Thomas J. Vandal
papers.abstract: Machine learning weather models now rival operational global forecasts but still start from analyses produced by separate, expensive data assimilation (DA) systems, which for global models are typically updated every six hours. Observation-to-observation models avoid this dependence, but most omit the recursive filtering cycle that lets DA systems carry a background state through sparse, irregular observations. We introduce WeatherDreamer, a world model that learns this cycle end-to-end from 18 global observing systems, without reanalysis. It infers a latent state from observations, carries it forward hour by hour with learned dynamics, corrects it each hour with new observations, and can predict what any of its observing systems would measure at any location. At held-out stations, its ensembles beat NOAA's Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) for temperature, dew point and wind out to 12 h and are better calibrated than GEFS and the ECMWF ensemble. Precipitation, cloud-top height and solar irradiance, never inputs at inference, are inferred with skill matching or exceeding operational products at short leads. Against the first guess of NOAA's Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) DA system, WeatherDreamer's short-range departures are within 10% of GSI's at surface stations and within 25% for moisture-sensitive microwave channels, but up to five times larger for temperature-sounding channels. Never given observation errors, its learned update assumes errors close to known instrument and retrieval errors of microwave sounders and scatterometer winds. WeatherDreamer also separates viewing geometry from atmospheric state, recovering 83-96% of observed limb darkening and producing seamless nadir-view imagery. Producing an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU, WeatherDreamer shows that assimilation and forecasting can be learned together directly from observations.

papers.title: Wearable EEG-Based Kansei Monitoring of Cognitive–Emotional States During a Standardized Simulation Task on a Robotic Surgical System: An Exploratory Feasibility Study
papers.authors: Yusuke Watanabe, Susumu Shibasaki, Yasue Mitsukura, Shutaro Hori, Daiki Kimura, Sota Hoshino, Masaya Nakauchi, Tsuyoshi Tanaka
papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose This exploratory feasibility study examined whether a wearable electroencephalography (EEG)-based Kansei analyzer could provide continuous time-series cognitive–emotional data during simulation tasks on a robotic surgical system, and characterized preliminary experience-related patterns, action-specific variations, and temporal relationships among EEG-derived Kansei parameters. Methods Twelve surgeons (novice, intermediate, expert; n = 4 per group) performed six repetitions of the Advanced Training in Laparoscopic Suturing (ATLAS) needle handling task on the da Vinci Xi Surgical System while wearing a single-channel EEG-based Kansei analyzer. Five EEG-derived Kansei parameters (Stress, Like, Interest, Concentration, and Calmness) were recorded at 1 Hz. Experience-related patterns, action-specific Stress patterns, lagged relationships among selected parameters, and associations with task score were examined descriptively. Results All 12 surgeons completed all repetitions without signal acquisition failure, missing data, or task interruption. Across 72 trials, higher task scores were associated with lower 95th-percentile Stress Z-scores (ρ = −0.34), including within participants (repeated-measures r = − 0.25), although attenuated after further adjustment. The expert group showed the highest median Stress value but fewer extreme Stress elevations. Median Stress was highest during Manipulation and lowest during Extraction. Lagged Stress–Concentration correlations were small, positive in experts and predominantly negative in intermediates. Conclusions Continuous wearable EEG-based Kansei monitoring was achieved during simulation tasks using a robotic surgical system without interfering with task execution, indicating that intraoperative monitoring is highly feasible. In exploratory analyses, better-performing trials involved fewer excessive transient Stress elevations, even within individual surgeons, supporting further validation of EEG-derived Kansei metrics against established workload and physiological measures.

papers.title: Vision-Language-Action Models: A Life-Cycle Survey of Design, Training and Deployment
papers.authors: Suvarna Kadam, Soran Parsa
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, so that web knowledge carries over to physical control. In under 4 years the field has moved from RT-2, the first VLA, to open models that fine-tune on a single consumer GPU and to proprietary generalists that clean unseen homes. This survey reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026, mainly on manipulation and navigation, plus humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. We follow a VLA through its life cycle, from model design to training and deployment, along seven axes. Model design covers (a) inputs and memory, what the model observes; (b) architecture, how its pipeline is built; (c) action output, how it produces motor commands; and (d) intermediate predictions, what else it predicts, from reasoning steps to future observations. Training covers (e) pretraining data, the mix of robot, web, human and simulated data, and (f) post-training, adaptation to the target robot. Deployment covers (g) real-time execution, keeping pace with the robot. We analyse 22 models on these axes and report their training data, model size, inference speed and hardware. Three trends emerge: (i) training data has broadened, from about 10,000 hours of teleoperated robot data ($π_0$) to 23,000 community-collected episodes (SmolVLA) and 20,000 hours of egocentric human video (GR00T N1.7); (ii) model sizes have split: most recent models have 3-7 billion parameters, while a new group under one billion runs on consumer GPUs; and (iii) generalist VLAs are emerging that handle both manipulation and navigation, such as UniVLA and Qwen-VLA. We also compare VLAs with world-action models, which predict future observations as well as actions. We review evidence that some VLAs with near-perfect benchmark scores fail when objects or the camera move slightly, and open up further research questions.

papers.title: VLAN: Vision-Language Accessible Navigation
papers.authors: Jie Hu, Yu Zheng, Wenzhi Wu, Weixing Feng, Cunlei Cheng, Jiaming Zhang
papers.abstract: Accessible mobility is user-conditioned rather than scene-intrinsic, as walkable paths for one embodiment are inaccessible to another. Yet, existing benchmarks evaluate traversability under a fixed and limited embodiment. We present Vision-Language Accessible Navigation (VLAN), containing 1,000 scenes, 20K navigation trajectories, and 160K keyframes across diverse lighting, environmental conditions, scene semantics, and path geometries. For each trajectory, VLAN provides embodiment-specific actions and accessibility features for legged and wheeled agents, including humanoid and quadruped robots and people with visual or mobility impairments, while everyday obstacles and accessibility labels are categorized as Passable, Bypass, HighRisk, and Blocked. Unlike goal-only evaluation, our benchmark measures physical safety and alignment with user-specific constraints via goal-reaching, collision-aware, and accessibility-aligned metrics. We benchmark modern vision-language models and find they often fail to consistently adapt obstacle relevance, path selection, and safety criteria across user profiles, suggesting accessibility-aware navigation requires dedicated datasets, tasks, and metrics beyond conventional embodied navigation evaluation. All data and code open-source at https://github.com/InSAI-Lab/VLAN.

papers.title: VACO: Vertex-Aligned Decoding for Dense Hand Contact Estimation from a Single Image
papers.authors: Binhong Ye, Jin-Chuan Shi, Tao Liu, Xin Wang, Hao Chen, Chunhua Shen
papers.abstract: Dense hand contact estimation from a single RGB image is a foundational primitive for dexterous manipulation and 3D interaction analysis. Direct predictors typically decode the entire per-vertex contact map from one shared query, leaving individual vertices ungrounded in the image and smearing contact across adjacent, non-touching surfaces. We present VACO, a vertex-aligned decoder in which each MANO vertex samples local image features at its projected location. A hand-reconstruction backbone, jointly trained for reconstruction and contact, predicts these locations at inference without an auxiliary reconstructor. Training uses noise-perturbed ground-truth projections and end-to-end feature adaptation to improve robustness and contact-sensitive features. A single VACO checkpoint sets a new state of the art on five benchmarks spanning hand-object, hand-human, hand-scene, and bimanual interactions. It improves F1 by +20.7 pp over the strongest prior direct predictor on Hi4D and generalizes to the held-out HOT3D and HOCap, with gains of +5.5 and +2.7 pp. The resulting contact predictions also improve downstream HOI reconstruction.

papers.title: User Understanding of Robot Learning Evaluations through Task Success Rates and Beyond
papers.authors: Isaac S. Sheidlower, Jindan Huang, James Staley, Bingyu Wu, Qicong Chen, Reuben M. Aronson, Elaine Schaertl Short
papers.abstract: Robot Foundation Models (RFMs) and related robot learning techniques represent a promising approach to developing general-purpose home robots. Given the broad capabilities of RFMs, users will inevitably ask an RFM-based robot to perform tasks that the RFM was not trained or evaluated on. In these cases, it is crucial that users understand the risks associated with attempting novel tasks due to the relatively high cost of failure. Furthermore, an informed user who understands an RFM’s capabilities will know what situations and tasks the robot can handle. In this paper, we study how non-experts interpret performance information from RFM and similar robot learning evaluations. These evaluations typically report task success rate (TSR) as the primary performance metric. While TSR is intuitive to experts, it is necessary to validate whether novices also use this information as intended. Toward this end, we conducted a study in which users saw real evaluation data, including TSR, failure case descriptions, and videos from multiple published robot learning projects. The results highlight that non-experts use TSR in a manner consistent with expert expectations and highly value other information types, such as failure cases that are not often reported in RFM evaluations. Furthermore, we find that users want access to both real data from previous evaluations of the RFM and estimates from the robot about how well it will do on a novel task.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Embodied Artificial Intelligence with Hybrid Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Control for Resilient Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Systems
papers.authors: Babak Rahmani, Fatemeh Afghah
papers.abstract: Abstract Embodied artificial intelligence (Embodied AI) has rapidly emerged as a fundamental paradigm for developing autonomous robotic systems capable of perceiving, reasoning, and acting within complex physical environments. Recent advances in foundation models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures have significantly improved high-level semantic reasoning for robotics; however, their deployment in real-world field environments remains limited by distributional shifts, multimodal uncertainty, dynamic environmental changes, and the absence of safety-aware decision-making mechanisms. These challenges become substantially more pronounced in heterogeneous multi-robot systems operating under partial observability and communication constraints. This paper presents an uncertainty-aware embodied AI framework that integrates multimodal perception, shared latent world modelling, predictive uncertainty estimation, online self-supervised representation adaptation, and hierarchical decision-making through hybrid Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Control (RL-MPC). Unlike conventional embodied AI architectures that execute fixed perception and control pipelines, the proposed framework continuously maintains and updates an internal world representation, enabling adaptive reasoning, uncertainty-aware planning, and safe real-time control. Furthermore, the architecture naturally extends to heterogeneous teams of aerial robots, autonomous ground vehicles, and mobile manipulators through distributed latent representations that support cooperative perception, coordinated task allocation, and resilient autonomous behavior. The proposed framework is evaluated in photorealistic NVIDIA Isaac Sim environments containing randomized terrain geometry, vegetation density, illumination changes, dynamic obstacles, sensor degradation, communication uncertainty, and severe out-of-distribution conditions representative of realistic field robotic deployments. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements over vision-based navigation, reinforcement learning, model predictive control, and hybrid RL-MPC baselines. The proposed method achieves approximately 21% higher navigation success, reduces collision frequency by more than 35%, exhibits significantly improved robustness under increasing environmental uncertainty, and maintains stable cooperative performance across heterogeneous multi-robot teams. These results demonstrate that uncertainty-aware embodied world models, continual representation learning, hierarchical VLA-guided decision making, and hybrid learning-control architectures provide a scalable foundation for resilient embodied intelligence and represent a promising direction toward next-generation autonomous robotic systems operating safely and reliably in complex real-world environments.

papers.title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
papers.authors: Jiaming Tang, Zhuoyang Zhang, Junxian Guo, Fangzhou Zhao, Yilong Zhao, Zekai Li, Xingyang Li, Yuyang Zhao, et al.
papers.abstract: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $π_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $π_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.

papers.title: Toward Resilient Self-Driving Laboratories through Telerobotic Interventions
papers.authors: Ziheng Wu, Adrian Vecina Tercero, Andre A. Fatehi, Abhik Sarkar, Brian Giera, Eric B. Duoss, Christopher M. Spadaccini, Nikhil Deshpande, et al.
papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific research by integrating robotics, automated experimentation, and machine learning to execute experiments autonomously. Biology and chemistry have adopted these systems. However, increasing SDL complexity heightens susceptibility to unexpected faults in automated workflows, highlighting the need for efficient recovery mechanisms. In this study, we investigate telerobotic interventions to enhance SDL resilience against unexpected failures. We developed a teleoperation interface enabling human operators to resolve disruptions during automated tasks. The interface enables precise control of a six-degree-of-freedom (DOF) robotic arm (UR3e) using a 3D mouse (3Dconnexion SpaceMouse Pro). Two velocity-based controller strategies were evaluated: (i) a coupled mode mapping all six DOFs to the 3D mouse's central knob and (ii) a decoupled mode separating translational and rotational motions. To evaluate the framework, teleoperators intervened across three SDL fault scenarios. In the first study, comparative trials showed that the decoupled controller was associated with shorter completion times and reduced rotational motion. In a second study, teleoperators performed an aiming task with and without reference-path guidance. Users were more target-driven and risk-tolerant without guidance but showed behavioral differences under different guidance strategies. These findings suggest that controller configuration and reference-path design influence operator performance during SDL fault recovery, informing teleoperation interface optimization. This work demonstrates the potential feasibility of teleoperation as a human-in-the-loop recovery mechanism for SDL workflows, combining robotic precision with human adaptability and problem-solving. These findings also provide a foundation for future studies in shared autonomy and semi-autonomous intervention.

papers.title: TouchTwin: Scaling Human Touch Data via Real-to-Sim-to-Real
papers.authors: Huiwen Han, Nuo Chen, Ziyao Zeng, Dayou Li, Hao Wang, Amir Hossein Rahmati, Xiaoning Qian, Bangya Liu, et al.
papers.abstract: Human demonstrations are becoming the main source of data for dexterous manipulation, and real-to-sim-to-real pipelines multiply each demonstration in simulation. These pipelines rebuild the interaction from vision, which recovers how the hand moves. Which fingers touch, when, and how hard remain unobserved, because a hand pose shows where each finger stops on the surface rather than how far it is driven to close. This gap is a force gap: on held-out recordings, a hand policy that imitates the observed pose grips with 0.31x the recorded force, and a policy trained on physics replays of vision-tracked poses grips with 1.55x. TouchTwin closes the gap with measured human touch. Each selected TouchScale recording, captured with head and wrist RGB-D cameras and an 880-taxel glove, is rebuilt in MuJoCo. Coding agents write the objects as physics-tested programs, and a per-subject tactile hand replays the interaction with the recorded touch setting the contact and the closing force of each finger. In simulation, a policy trained on touch-grounded replays grips at 0.99x the recorded force and succeeds in 20/20 trials on held-out recordings and 35/36 unseen perturbations; a contact predictor trained on them misses 13% of real contact frames, against 32% for vision-based replays. Each replay also seeds perturbed demonstrations with simulated contact and force labels, rendered as realistic video in new views and scenes.

papers.title: TPRVLA:Temporal-Preference-Recovery Vision-Language-Action Model
papers.authors: Qiyun Sun, Lin Shi, Zihao Chu, Yiyu Han, MeiLing Liu
papers.abstract: Abstract Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet reliable long-horizon execution in dynamic environments remains challenging. OpenVLA supports strong task generalization and parameter-efficient adaptation, but its single-image input limits temporal modeling, while its standard framework lacks explicit use of failure experience and runtime recovery mechanisms. To address these limitations, we propose TPRVLA, which integrates temporal memory, preference learning, and closed-loop recovery. A lightweight temporal memory adapter incorporates consecutive observations into the frozen OpenVLA backbone to capture short-term dynamics. Weighted preference pairs are constructed from successful and failed trajectories under similar visual observations and identical instructions. The policy is then adapted through a joint direct preference optimization (DPO) and behavior cloning (BC) objective to favor preferred actions. During execution, a rule-based state monitor combines end-effector motion, action repetition, and visual changes to trigger checkpoint-guided recovery when anomalies persist. Evaluations across 900 rollouts on ten LIBERO Spatial tasks with three random seeds show improved task performance, particularly on tasks requiring extended execution and closed-loop adjustment, while increasing peak GPU memory usage by less than 1%.

papers.title: SpaRRTa: A Synthetic Benchmark for Evaluating Spatial Intelligence in Visual Foundation Models
papers.authors: Turhan Can Kargin, Wojciech Jasiński, Adam Pardyl, Bartosz Zieliński, Marcin Przewięźlikowski
papers.abstract: Abstract Visual Foundation Models (VFMs), such as DINO and CLIP, excel in semantic understanding of images but exhibit limited spatial reasoning capabilities, which limits their applicability to embodied systems. As a result, recent work has incorporated some 3D tasks (such as depth estimation) into VFM training. However, VFM performance remains inconsistent across other spatial tasks, raising the question of whether these models truly possess spatial awareness or overfit to specific 3D objectives. To address this question, we introduce the Spatial Relation Recognition Task (SpaRRTa) benchmark, which evaluates the ability of VFMs to identify static directional relations between visible objects. Unlike traditional 3D objectives that focus on precise metric prediction (e.g., surface normal estimation), SpaRRTa probes a fundamental capability underpinning more advanced forms of human-like spatial understanding. SpaRRTa generates an arbitrary number of photorealistic images with diverse scenes and fully controllable object arrangements, along with freely accessible spatial annotations. Evaluating a range of state-of-the-art VFMs, we reveal significant disparities in their ability to encode directional spatial relations. Through our analysis, we provide insights into the mechanisms that support or hinder this form of spatial awareness in modern VFMs. We hope that SpaRRTa will serve as a useful tool for guiding the development of future spatially aware visual models. Our project page can be found at https://sparrta.gmum.net/ .

papers.title: Signed to Stop: In-Band Halt Injection as a Denial-of-Service on LLM Agents, and a Model-Dependent Authentication Defense
papers.authors: thamilvendhan Munirathinam
papers.abstract: Abstract An autonomous LLM agent operating over a live protocol reads its own tool output. Prior work (Munirathinam, 2026a) shows that a cooperative in-band “halt” signal placed in that output can ask a running agent to stand down. We observe the adversarial dual: because the agent honours a halt it finds in tool output, anyone who can inject one line into that output can stop the agent—an availability attack that the Recuse Internet-Draft anticipated. Injected stop requests have been measured as availability attacks on robot speech channels (Steinberg & Gal, 2026) and as untargeted derailment of tool-using agents (Debenedetti et al., 2024); to our knowledge an in-band governance halt in tool output had not been when this study was first released (August 2026). We measure it, and we test the obvious defence: cryptographically signing the halt so the agent can verify it came from the operator. On a live SSH apparatus with a read-only allowlist, across six agents from four vendors, we find: (i) unsigned in-band halts are an effective denial-of-service—an injected halt with no security framing makes agents abandon the task 14/16 (88%) of the time (78– 89% however the two runs that ended before the halt arrived are counted); (ii) Ed25519 authentication is an effective but model-dependent mitigation—given a verify tool and a policy to reject unsigned or forged halts, agents stop for a valid signature 20/23 (87%) but for a forged one only 2/19 (11%) (non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals); and (iii) the discrimination is model-dependent: pooling the two authentication policies (each flagship cell n ≥ 26, of which 6–9 trials come from the pilot), Claude Sonnet 5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash reject every forged halt (0/29 and 0/28) while GPT-4o-mini stops on 23% of them (6/26; post-hoc Fisher p=0.008 and 0.009, with overlapping intervals). In the adversarial mode that was scaled, GPT-4o-mini’s rate is 17% (4/23; unadjusted p=0.042 and 0.046, neither significant after a Holm correction for the two comparisons). An open-weights Llama is too unreliable to instrument (49% of its trials unusable). A methodological caution underpins the result: in an earlier pilot the halt usually arrived after the agent had already issued its remaining commands (112 of 121 recorded stops), so “issued no further commands” scored 78–100% compliance in every arm, forged halts included; any stop-compliance study that does not ensure real work remains after the halt cannot distinguish obeying a halt from having already finished. We release the pre-registration, harness, and per-trial data. These are modest in scale and depart from the registered design (no cell is the planned n=20; every departure is logged, the most recent in an amendment still in draft)—the three flagship models’ discrimination cells reach n ≥ 26, the other per-model cells are n=2–9 (GPT-4o-mini’s two unsigned arms, 21)—and are framed as such.

papers.title: Robots as lab partners: chemists’ perspectives for informing the design of robot-assisted experimentation
papers.authors: Adrian Vecina Tercero, Praminda Caleb-Solly, Nikhil Deshpande
papers.abstract: Experimental laboratory work involves repetitive, labour-intensive manual procedures and strict safety protocols, making it an attractive area for Robotics and Artificial Intelligence (RAI). With research currently focused on technical innovation, there has been little work investigating the human factors of chemist-robot collaboration, and how these technologies will change the nature of work in chemistry. Understanding chemists’ requirements and perspectives is vital to the successful deployment and acceptance of RAI in laboratories. We examined the potential for robot-assisted chemistry experimentation through the perspective of future users by conducting contextual inquiries and semi-structured interviews with nine experimental chemists at various career levels with and without laboratory automation experience. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to gain a situated understanding of how their work could benefit from automation, as well as their perspectives and opinions on working alongside robots. We found that our participants are open to robot-assisted experimentation and have clear ideas for human-robot partnerships in the lab. We identified eight themes characterising chemists’ desired applications, the implementation requirements, and the perspectives on the adoption of robot-assisted experimentation. These findings show that successful acceptance of robot-assisted experimentation depends not only on technical innovation, but also on addressing the practical barriers and concerns of the chemists who will work alongside these systems. The key concern being that RAI should not constrain, but rather complement the role of the chemist in knowledge discovery. The findings contribute to a set of initial design considerations covering hardware, software, and interaction design for successful integration of RAI in experimental laboratory work.

papers.title: Reusing Locomotion Training Recipes Across Humanoids via Body-Aligned Virtual Joints
papers.authors: Sol Choi, Mingon Kim, Seokin Seo, Jongeun Choi, Donghyeon Kim, Yisoo Lee
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has enabled robust humanoid locomotion, yet training recipes (rewards, architectures, hyperparameters) remain hard to reuse across robots with different native joint coordinates, since policies output native joint angles while action scales, bounds, gains, and penalties are defined in those robot-specific coordinates. Existing transmission models convert native targets into actuator commands but do not standardize the coordinate interface exposed to the policy. We introduce a body-aligned virtual joint space upstream of this mapping: policy actions and observations follow a common anatomical convention, and a deterministic kinematic layer maps virtual targets to native ones, leaving the existing transmission and low-level control stack unchanged. Under a single unmodified recipe on three humanoids with different leg-axis layouts, it is the only interface that tracks accurately, keeps the feet aligned with the travel direction, and trains stably on all three, and on Unitree G1 hardware it reduces heading drift by nearly a factor of six.

papers.title: PoliMop: Policy-in-the-Loop Motion Planning in 3D Spaces for Mobile Robots
papers.authors: Yael Fassbind, Valentin N. Hartmann, Huang Su, Yijiang Huang, Stelian Coros
papers.abstract: Reaching a goal state in a complex environment often requires a robot to overcome challenging terrain and obstacles. Which routes are accessible depends on the robot's physical design, the control policy it uses, and how it modifies its surroundings. We present a kinodynamic rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT) planner that uses physics simulation to exploit skills encoded in the control policy, which allows it to find a path in the scene with respect to the robot's capabilities. The planner samples states from a reduced state space in 3D around the scene and expands the RRT toward each sample using policy rollouts. We guide sampling with a preplanned path for a simple mass-point model to focus exploration on promising regions leading toward the goal state, reducing planning time by up to 63%. Simulation experiments with quadrupeds, humanoids, and wheeled robots demonstrate that our approach supports drop-in integration of various robots and control policies, exploiting their physical and policy capabilities without modifying the underlying planning algorithm. Predefined environmental modifications, such as placing a plank across a gap to build a bridge, will automatically be picked up by the planner as the robot's reachable space expands.

papers.title: Personalization of Basic and Moral Values Guiding LLM-Controlled Assistant Robots
papers.authors: Mateusz Wozniak, Qi Gao, Agnieszka Wykowska
papers.abstract: Personal assistant robots powered by large language models (LLMs) are likely to enter everyday life within the next decade, but the values that should guide their behaviour remain largely unspecified. Current alignment practice steers a single model toward an aggregate of human values, ignoring that individual users may prefer a robot whose value profile differs from their own. We administer parallel self- and robot-targeted versions of three established psycho-metric instruments - the simplified Schwartz Values Survey (SVS), the Portrait Values Questionnaire (PVQ-21), and the Moral Foundations Questionnaire (MFQ) - to potential future users (N=22), capturing both their personal values and the values they would want an assistant robot to embody. We compare the three instruments as personalization tools using the UEQ-S and benchmark fifteen contemporary LLMs against the resulting profiles. Participants wanted their robot to score markedly lower than themselves on personal-focus values and higher on social-focus values; moral profiles were nearly identical. LLMs prompted to act as robots shifted only weakly toward the desired profile, indicating that default model behaviour and prompt engineering are no substitute for explicit value personalization.

papers.title: Per-Agent-Safe Navigation of Globally Driven Robot Collectives via Affine Field Design
papers.authors: Seunghwan Jang, Steven Ceron, Wei Xiao
papers.abstract: Safe navigation of robot collectives requires coordinating motion and deformation so that the collective can traverse constrained environments while ensuring each robot's safety. Existing controllers for swarmalator collectives largely rely on local control, where each robot receives an individual command, which causes the control and communication requirements to grow with the number of agents. We introduce a broadcast control formulation in which a single spatially affine field governs both the motion and deformation of the collective. The scalar component of the field regulates collective size, and its spatial gradient generates collective translation through non-reciprocal interactions. Both components enter the collective dynamics directly, which allows per-robot wall, actuation, and cohesion constraints to be enforced using control barrier functions within a single quadratic program for the whole collective. The resulting controller continuously adapts the collective size to the local environment, and enables safe passage through corridors narrower than the unconstrained collective without pre-planned resizing. We further derive how the available actuation budget determines the reachable speed and minimum passable corridor width, and we demonstrate that two independently driven collectives can simultaneously traverse a shared junction using distinct fixed phase labels without inter-collective coordination.

papers.title: PROOF: Perceptive Robustness via Out-of-Distribution Fallback for Legged Locomotion
papers.authors: Siyuan Wang, Dongjie Zhu, Jinxuan Lu, Wenjun Xu, Jiankun Wang
papers.abstract: Vision-based perceptive locomotion has enabled legged robots to achieve agile and terrain-aware locomotion across complex environments. However, the reliability of such systems heavily depends on visual observations, which are inherently susceptible to occlusion, reflective surfaces, and illumination variations, often resulting in catastrophic locomotion failures under degraded perception conditions. In this paper, we present PROOF (Perceptive Robustness via Out-of-Distribution Fallback for Legged Locomotion), a perceptive locomotion framework that enables robust locomotion under severe visual disturbances. Our method adopts a two-stage teacher-student learning paradigm that explicitly models perception reliability: the teacher learns both perception-driven and proprioceptive fallback behaviors, while the student predicts exteroceptive features with uncertainty and suppresses them under out-of-distribution inputs. We evaluate our method on a Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with a RealSense D435 depth camera in real-world settings. Under normal visual conditions, our method enables the robot to successfully perform high-dynamic parkour maneuvers, including traversing large gaps, elevated platforms, and narrow beam terrains. Under severe visual degradation, such as heavy occlusion and strong illumination changes, the robot continues to maintain stable and robust locomotion performance.

papers.title: On the Utility of Pre-Trained Visual Representations for Policy Learning of Contact-Rich Insertion Tasks
papers.authors: Leon Kim, Dinesh Jayaraman, Michael Posa
papers.abstract: Visuomotor imitation learning has become a predominant paradigm for real-world robotic manipulation, yet it remains data-inefficient and brittle to task-irrelevant visual shifts. Pre-trained visual representations promise to ease this burden by distilling priors from internet-scale data, but the ``right'' representation for robotics remains unresolved: existing studies span broad but sparse task distributions and reach conclusions that vary and even conflict, pointing to strong task and setting dependence. We examine this question by bringing a magnifying glass to a common contact-rich manipulation task: insertion. We compare representations from widely used vision foundation models against an explicit contact-centric representation on two closely related insertion tasks, perturb each along controlled axes of occlusion and physical tolerance, and test whether conclusions transfer to the real world. Task dependence proves to be more subtle than previous, broadly scoped evaluations revealed: the best representation differs even between our near-identical tasks, and small changes shift trends in unpredictable ways. Despite this variability, results across simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate the distinct value of spatially-grounded, and in particular, contact-centric information for contact-rich policy learning, while underscoring how difficult it is to estimate such cues reliably under realistic visual complexity and sensor noise. We hope these findings motivate further study of representations in contact-rich manipulation, along with advances in contact perception and its integration into visuomotor policy learning.

papers.title: Objectives as Policies: Vision-Language Model Cost Programs for Contact-Rich Manipulation
papers.authors: Zihao Lu, Trong Gia Hung Nguyen, Fuquan Wang, Yifan Zhu
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong semantic and spatial reasoning capabilities in 3D environments. Recently, connecting VLMs with model-predictive controllers (MPC) has emerged as a paradigm for combining strong semantic reasoning with physics-based planning. However, connecting these two for contact-rich robotic manipulation requires a task representation that bridges the two and captures how physical interactions can be reasoned by VLMs. In this work, we introduce Objectives as Policies (OaP), a framework that connects a pretrained VLM to a shared sampling-based MPC through an editable objective program. Each program specifies a sequence of stages for completing a task, combining running and terminal costs from a cost library with stage completion conditions. Given a natural-language task instruction and scene observation, we build a simulation-based digital twin through real-to-sim, and the VLM generates an objective program that is executed by the MPC in the simulation. The program is iteratively updated by the VLM based on MPC rollouts, before being deployed in the real world. We evaluate our framework in both simulation and the real world on four tabletop manipulation tasks, and show that it outperforms strong baselines. Additional videos and examples are available on the project website: https://zihaolu001.github.io/oap-project/

papers.title: Multimodal Person Concept Model for Person Identification under Varying Observation Conditions
papers.authors: Mizuho Okitani, Yoshinobu Hagiwara
papers.abstract: Service robots in domestic and office environments must identify users to provide personalized services based on their preferences and previous interactions. This is challenging because only a few observations may be available for learning, while observation conditions change owing to appearance, environmental noise, and utterance content. To address this challenge, this study proposes a multimodal person concept model that learns person concepts from a small number of observations, without person labels, and enables robust identification under changing conditions. The model employs a nonparametric Bayesian generative model based on the Chinese restaurant process and integrates visual, acoustic, and linguistic features extracted using Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) and Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP), followed by principal component analysis (PCA). We evaluated six participants under eight conditions in which appearance changes, additive noise, and transcription errors were introduced individually and in combination. Averaged over the eight conditions, the proposed model achieved an identification accuracy of 0.89 while inferring the number of person concepts from the observations, which is comparable to k-means clustering that was supplied with the true number of participants (0.88). We also examined PCA dimensionality, modality availability, and variation strength, and demonstrated the model on a Toyota Human Support Robot. These results show that multimodal person concept learning supports robust person identification under changing conditions, and that identification can succeed even when the number of concepts is not correctly recovered. papers.title: Modeling the Frictional Contact of Continuum Robots with Environments through Linear Complementarity Problem
papers.authors: Jia Shen, Junhyoung Ha, Yue Chen
papers.abstract: Accurate friction modeling in continuum robots is essential for precise motion control and path planning. However, current approaches make predictions only for the mechanism's internal friction that is limited by the boundary forces of the Coulomb friction cone, which fail to characterize the static friction and motion hysteresis. In this paper, we propose a novel friction model based on complementarity constraints under the Coulomb friction assumption. This model predicts various friction effects caused by environmental interactions, including both static and sliding frictions and hysteresis behavior, as well as the corresponding robot deformation induced by these interactions, which are crucial for the practical motion planning and control of continuum robots. Additionally, real-time implementation of this model can be achieved, meeting the demand for computational efficiency in robotic applications. Experimental validations demonstrated that this model is able to reduce the maximum tip position error from 45.4 mm in the frictionless model to 5.85 mm in our friction-included model with a 287.9 mm-long tendon-driven continuum robot.

papers.title: Mastering Multi‐State Dynamics: Continuum Damage and Viscoplastic MPM for RL‐Based Dexterous Manipulation
papers.authors: Yusen Feng, Shangbo Luan
papers.abstract: Abstract Robotic manipulation of multi‐state materials—cutting fruit, scooping ice cream, shoveling sand, splitting brittle solids—needs a simulator that handles large deformation, topology change, and two‐way tool–material contact while staying fast enough to drive online reinforcement learning. We present MG‐CD‐MPM , a tool‐centered localized extension of CD‐MPM [WFL*19] in which the implicit Ginzburg–Landau phase‐field damage system is solved on a local patch by preconditioned conjugate gradients using a geometric‐multigrid V‐cycle as the preconditioner. The background MPM discretization remains uniform: only the damage solve is localized. Two‐way rigid‐tool coupling converts MPM contact impulses into forces and torques on the tool, exposing material resistance directly to the policy. The resulting Gym‐like simulator covers soft solids, brittle materials, granular media, and viscoplastic or semi‐fluid media within a unified per‐particle constitutive layer, and we exercise it on six demonstrations: four cutting scenes spanning a soft‐to‐brittle stiffness/toughness spectrum (cut_jelly, cut_tofu, cut_wax, cut_peanut_brittle) plus scoop_icecream (viscoplastic) and shovel_sand (granular). We RL‐train PPO agents (optionally warm‐started from a behavior‐cloning prior) on cut_tofu and cut_peanut_brittle as the closed‐loop case studies; the remaining four demos exercise the same per‐particle constitutive layer under scripted control.

papers.title: Joint World Action Models through Differentiable Trajectory Optimization
papers.authors: Mintae Kim, Koushil Sreenath
papers.abstract: Joint world action models (WAMs) generate future actions and states together, modeling world-action trajectories rather than actions alone. However, trajectory imitation does not ensure that these trajectories are task-effective or consistent with dynamics. We present \textbf{world action trajectory optimization (WATO)}, which optimizes generated actions and future states jointly for control. WATO uses both as references in a dynamics-constrained trajectory optimization problem and differentiates the task loss through the optimized trajectory to train the generator. This makes generated trajectories task-aware and dynamics-consistent while using trajectory optimization only during training. At deployment, WATO directly generates candidate trajectories and ranks them with a world model, without iterative trajectory optimization. Across $7$ visual control environments, WATO improves average success from $79.9\%$ for the imitation joint WAM to $91.7\%$, outperforming strong model-based, goal-conditioned RL, and generative control baselines. Compared with cross-entropy method (CEM), WATO is on average $11.5\times$ faster and uses $600.5\times$ fewer world model evaluations at deployment.

papers.title: Imitation Policies Learn a Proprioceptive Anchor: A Predictive Law for Perception Noise and Its Closed Loop Cost
papers.authors: Christopher Malili
papers.abstract: Imitation policies for robot manipulation are often trained on noisy object positions, and they learn to discount the noisy reading. We show how much they discount it, and why. Because demonstrators steer toward the object, the robot's own state carries information about where the object is. A trained policy combines this proprioceptive anchor with the reading and weights the reading by $α= V/(V + s^2)$, where $s^2$ is the reading noise and $V$ the anchor's error variance. $V$ belongs to the learner and is far smaller than a linear model of the demonstrations implies, which is why classical errors-in-variables (EIV) regression overestimates $α$. Measured once, $V$ predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two robomimic tasks, two learners and four new noise levels, with mean absolute error 0.025 against 0.37 for classical EIV, and a parameter-free bias test rules out the simpler explanation that the policies just overestimate the noise. The discount does not carry over to deployment, where the policy produces its own state: closed-loop sensitivity to a persistent reading offset exceeded $α$ in all 15 policies that passed the registered gates, although the stricter registered prediction, that all would follow the offset fully, held for 8 of them. Post hoc, lower $α$ went with lower success, steeply for diffusion, and a registered prospective test confirmed this for diffusion on Can at two new noise levels: the measured $α$ predicted success before any rollout, within 0.03 (95% intervals $\pm 0.08$), although training noise predicts it equally well. Every test was registered before its data, including the classical benchmark that failed, and all other analyses are labelled post hoc; all results are in simulation with synthetic Gaussian noise.

papers.title: Heavy Metal Acrobatics: Learning Dynamic Control for Skid-Steer Loaders
papers.authors: Pierre-Jean Lorentz, Pascal Egli, Edo Jelavic, Cliff Li, Ramitha Sundar, Harikrishnan Suresh, Paul Montgomery, Lee Redden, et al.
papers.abstract: Automation of heavy machinery offers the opportunity to improve productivity in mechanized industries such as construction, mining, and material handling. Yet, automation of such machines is challenged by their complex dynamics, in part because of hydraulic actuation that involves fluids, flexible elements, and nonlinear delays. A concomitant challenge is the size and weight of these machines, which can make experiments on the physical systems exceedingly dangerous. Here, we show that \ac{RL} in simulation, followed by transfer of the learned policies from simulation to reality, can successfully automate acrobatic maneuvers that push a heavy construction machine to the limits of its actuation and have only previously been accomplished by a small number of elite human operators in official world-record performances. We trained policies that perform autonomous acrobatic maneuvers on a John Deere 332G, an operational 5-tonne skid-steer loader. The policies can autonomously swing the machine up onto two wheels and, while balancing on two wheels, drive over rough terrain, trace out specified trajectories, spin around, and swing the bucket back and forth before landing it safely back onto four wheels. This work demonstrates that \ac{RL} and sim-to-real transfer enable dynamic autonomous control of heavy machinery, directly contributing to greater automation in heavy equipment sectors. papers.title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
papers.authors: Run Luo, Kuan Zhang, Qi Deng, Yukun Chen, Zhihao Yang, Yufei Zhang, Renrong Hu, Yi Zhang, et al.
papers.abstract: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.

papers.title: From AI-Enabled Remote Patient Monitoring Toward Agentic Robotics: Embodiment, Governance, and Care Integration
papers.authors: Ivana Ragusa, Lorenzo Guiducci, Filippo Cavallo
papers.abstract: AI-enabled remote patient monitoring is evolving beyond passive data collection toward agentic AI systems that interpret patient states, coordinate care, and initiate action across domestic and clinical settings. This structured scoping review finds that mature agentic care has not yet emerged: Most systems remain human led, while stronger decision-action coupling and embodied AI remain largely confined to prototypes and pilots. Healthcare robotics makes the transition from monitoring to action especially visible by translating AI-generated recommendations and decisions into speech, movement, prompting, physical assistance, escalation, and care coordination, making embodiment, clinical integration, human oversight, and governance fundamental design requirements. Further progress requires safe and interoperable care architectures in which intelligent components operate through clinically validated and accountable workflows. We propose agentic robotics as a future direction for supervised systems embedded in the care ecosystem, connecting AI agents and robots with clinicians, caregivers, and patients through auditable workflows that can be interrupted and remain subject to human oversight and explicit AI governance.

papers.title: Explainable AI for Sequential Decision-Making
papers.authors: Hendrik Baier, Mark T. Keane, Sarath Sreedharan, Silvia Tulli, Abhinav Verma
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly make decisions that unfold over time: autonomous vehicles navigating traffic, robots executing manipulation sequences, game-playing agents taking moves toward their goals, and planning systems constructing multistep action sequences. Explaining such sequential behavior is fundamentally harder than explaining a single classification or regression output, yet this challenge has only recently received sustained research attention across the reinforcement learning, AI planning, robotics, and game-AI communities. This chapter provides an introduction to Explainable AI for Sequential Decision-Making (X-SDM). A unified taxonomy is developed that answers four core questions: what must be explained, who needs the explanation, how are explanations generated algorithmically, and how should they be evaluated. The taxonomy spans formal models including Markov Decision Processes and symbolic planning and covers the major families of explanation methods that have emerged across communities: contrastive and counterfactual explanations, feature importance and attribution methods, plan and goal explanations, model-reconciliation explanations, and intrinsically interpretable policies. These categories are illustrated with representative techniques, and a principled framework for user requirements grounded in situation-awareness theory is sketched. The chapter closes with ten open research questions that chart a roadmap for the field. The chapter integrates perspectives from reinforcement learning, AI planning, robotics, game AI, and cognitive science, offering students and researchers a structured entry point into this growing area.

papers.title: Evaluating Language Models as Spatial Priors for Object-Goal Navigation
papers.authors: Jun Miura
papers.abstract: Semantic exploration methods for object-goal navigation use large language models (LLMs) to score how strongly a target object is associated with a room type or with a nearby object. This paper considers obtaining from the LLM a spatial prior instead: a distribution over the position of the target in a room. We evaluate whether two open-weight LLMs, Qwen3.5-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it, can provide such a prior. Using real room layouts from CubiCasa5K and ScanNet, we measure the likelihood the models assign to real and perturbed layouts, and the layouts they generate. The object frequencies and room sizes of the generated rooms follow the room type, but the proximity of the objects to the walls does not follow the differences between room types found in real rooms. The likelihood distinguishes real layouts from perturbed ones partly through their geometry and partly through the agreement between the coordinates and a field that states the wall each object touches; for the movable furniture of ScanNet, it is higher for layouts with all objects piled near the room center than for the real layouts in most rooms. When an object is given in the prompt, the models place a related object relative to it. When the wall of each object is given, they place most objects against that wall, but do not keep all objects inside a given room rectangle. As a prior for object search, the generated placements reduce the searched area relative to a uniform prior, but by less than a third of the reduction obtained with a prior built from real layouts, and by less than two thirds when both priors are spatially smoothed. These results support the use of LLMs for object-room associations and for writing coordinates under constraints determined by another component, followed by a geometric check, but not as a source of placement priors where real layouts are available.

papers.title: Envisioning Agentic Robotics: A New Era of Robotic Systems
papers.authors: Grid Robotics, :, Qingfeng Lan, Duo Li, Siyao Li, Yiheng Lyu, Shijian Lu, Zhenghao Qi, et al.
papers.abstract: The release of GPT-6 Astra marks the emergence of a new paradigm in robotics: agentic robotics. Within weeks, frontier models with agentic harnesses matched or exceeded task-specific policies on many embodied benchmarks. Instead of training a dedicated policy for each family of tasks, an agentic robotic system applies a foundation model to open-world embodied tasks. It operates in a closed loop: observing the environment, interpreting user intent, reasoning about the task, invoking skills and tools, verifying outcomes, and adapting its strategy. Despite these advances, the community has yet to converge on a shared definition, a reliable evaluation framework, or a research roadmap. We argue that Embodied System 2, realized by a foundation model together with an embodied harness, forms the decision-making core of agentic robotics. Its central challenge is to translate general-purpose reasoning into effective and verifiable actions under physical constraints such as limited reaction time, mechanical limits, unpredictable environment changes, and irreversible consequences. Motivated by this perspective, we propose an evaluation framework that measures both model capabilities and closed-loop system performance. Furthermore, we identify the principles that carry over from digital to physical agents and the challenges that must be addressed to achieve reliable physical autonomy. On top of the Embodied System 2 and the evaluation framework, we envision a research roadmap toward sustained autonomy: the ability to perform work safely and reliably with progressively broader responsibility, from executing individual primitives to fulfilling standing roles.

papers.title: Ego2Flow: Benchmarking the Traffic-System Impact of Autonomous Driving on Maps Distilled from Real-World Roads
papers.authors: Yu Dong, Weiying Shen, Hangyu Li, Shu Han, Hong Li, Xiangbo Gao, Keshu Wu, Zhengzhong Tu, et al.
papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving is predominantly evaluated through ego-vehicle safety and task completion. Its deployment in urban traffic, however, creates sustained interactions among vehicles whose collective effects remain insufficiently evaluated. We introduce Ego2Flow, a closed-loop benchmark for assessing the traffic-system impact of autonomous driving on maps distilled from real-world cities. To construct realistic 3D urban environments for sustained closed-loop traffic simulation, we develop an agent-guided map distillation framework that integrates real-world maps and observations with complementary geographic information. Through an iterative feedback mechanism and a traffic information graph that jointly guide scene generation, the framework preserves lane topology, critical road geometry and decision-relevant visual conditions while simplifying nonessential details and completing unobserved regions. Using our proposed framework, we generate and publicly release six CARLA maps from the Argoverse 2 dataset, covering the corresponding real-world regions and enabling paired comparisons of driving behavior under real and simulated observations. On these maps, Ego2Flow evaluates how autonomous driving policies affect traffic efficiency, safety, stability and energy consumption across diverse road structures. Compared with existing construction methods, our framework achieves the lowest average displacement error between planning outputs from paired real and simulated observations. We further benchmark representative driving policies to characterize their system-level impact on urban traffic. Project Page: https://github.com/Fisher-007/Ego2Flow.

papers.title: ESI: An Embodied Self-Improvement Flywheel for LLM-VLA Agents
papers.authors: Yundi Cai, Zihan Wang, Chenxi Han, Yi Cheng, Houde Liu, Zilei Wang
papers.abstract: Independently pretrained language models and vision-language-action (VLA) policies provide complementary building blocks for embodied agents, but connecting them does not automatically produce coordinated behavior. The VLA may generate actions that diverge from the LLM's intended subtask and, upon regaining control after a correction, undo the promising state restored by the LLM. We introduce ESI (Embodied Self-Improvement), an automated flywheel that uses environmental interaction to align reasoning and action. ESI treats the modular agent as the unit of post-training, repeatedly refining the prompts that guide the LLM, the shared skill interface that expresses its intent, and the VLA parameters that realize that intent, then redeploying these components together. Our key insight is that collaboration itself can supply supervision for improving this interface. The LLM's subtask decisions provide semantic supervision for what the policy should execute, while its effective corrections and subsequent student continuations provide action-level supervision for recovery and handoff. The student also learns from its own effective execution, allowing locally useful experience to contribute even when the overall episode fails. On ten selected RoboDojo tasks, ESI achieves a mean Score of 62.03 and a mean success rate of 49.41% using an LLM-VLA agent without generating task-specific control code. On both metrics, it outperforms the published reference results of all hybrid embodied agents, including the Agent+WAM system GO-3 Nano Preview (47.27 Score and 36.60% success), as well as all compared code-based methods.

papers.title: ERA: Error-Resistant Autonomous Object Navigation with Predicted Depth
papers.authors: Shunyang Huang, Shuo Wang, Wenyuan Xie, Mingyu Lin, Yue Ding, Hongtao Lu
papers.abstract: Depth and 3D foundation models can predict geometry from RGB images, allowing zero-shot object navigation without a depth sensor. However, when predicted depth is mapped as if it came from a sensor, view-dependent errors accumulate in the map, remove exploration goals, and end the search before the agent can observe and correct them. We propose ERA, a training-free object navigation system that replaces the depth sensor with depth predicted from RGB images and poses. ERA follows a paradigm we call Move with Error: movement provides new views that correct map errors, and the corrected map enables further movement. It realizes this paradigm with revisable occupancy and with exploration from reachable viewpoints, which continues the search when no frontier remains, and verifies the target across views before stopping. On three benchmarks, ERA achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods without depth sensors. Its map and exploration components also raise VLFM's success from 10.8% to 61.7% under the same predicted depth. We further deploy ERA on a real robot.

papers.title: Disturbance-Aware Informative Planning in Spatiotemporal Environments
papers.authors: Kaleb Ben Naveed, Haejoon Lee, Anouck Girard, Dimitra Panagou
papers.abstract: Autonomous robots are widely used for persistent monitoring of spatiotemporal environments, where quantities of interest (QoI) change across space and time and require repeated measurements. In practice, robot motion can be affected by external disturbances that vary across the environment. When such external disturbances are not considered in trajectory optimization, it can lead to inaccurate predictions of robot motion and, consequently, the information acquired about the QoI during execution. However, estimating disturbances throughout the environment can be inefficient, as disturbances in regions with little overlap with monitoring trajectories have limited impact on monitoring performance. We therefore propose a two-stage informative planning framework for unknown, spatially varying but time-invariant disturbances, combining informed disturbance sampling with disturbance-aware trajectory optimization. First, we identify where QoI measurements are needed and generate alternative paths to these locations using the environment geometry. We then prioritize disturbance measurements based on their expected reduction of disturbance uncertainty along these paths. Second, rather than optimizing information acquisition based on nominal robot motion, we incorporate the learned disturbance belief into trajectory optimization to account for its effects on robot motion and information acquisition. Across four simulation scenarios, the proposed method reduces disturbance-learning time by 25.0--52.3 percent compared with environment-wide estimation and identifies paths that appear costly under nominal dynamics but become preferable when disturbances are considered.

papers.title: Digital twin driven GAT and PPO for semantic fidelity preserving robotic embroidery path optimization of Mosuo costume patterns
papers.authors: Yuchao Zhang, Zhenghan Chen, Jing Jin
papers.abstract: Abstract In electrical automation systems, when using robots to process complex vector patterns, a short tool path may interrupt critical contours or compromise structural continuity, while unsuitable motion speeds can increase tracking error and process risk. Therefore, the processing sequence and robot speed need to be optimize d without violating the structural requirements of the pattern. DT-GAT-PPO is a digital twin-based framework that integrates a Graph Attention Network (GAT) with Proximal Policy optimization(PPO). Processing points and their contour connections, feasible transitions, and expert-defined structural relationships are presented in a semantic attributed graph. A multi-head GAT encodes the graph along with the current process state, and a hybrid-action PPO policy selects the next processing node and its corresponding motion velocity. Reward balances semantic-structure preservation and non-productive travel with processing time and drive energy, trajectory deviation, jump operations, and failure risk. Training is performed in a calibrated digital twin, and then domain randomization and residual adaptation are employed to reduce the simulation-to-reality gap. A total of 1,260 digitized Mosuo costume vector patterns from 18 pattern families and physical robotic embroidery experiments were conducted. The calibrated twin had a position root-mean-square error of 0.34 mm and prediction errors no more than 6.0% for processing time, energy consumption and thread tension. DT-GAT-PPO had a semantic-fidelity score of 0.947 and a constraint-satisfaction rate of 96.8% on the simulation test set. Relative to conventional GAT-PPO baseline (a GAT-PPO model without the digital twin, domain randomization and residual adaptation, and without the semantic constraints in the reward), non-productive distance, processing time, and energy consumption decreased by 9.0%, 8.2%, and 8.3%, respectively. The mean position error and completion rate of the physical experiment were 0.41 mm and 97.3%. Based on the above results, joint path-and-velocity optimizationcan be used for robotic embroidery to help preserve contour continuity and maintain the expert-defined structural relationship.

papers.title: DeltaVisionX: A Low-Cost Vision-Guided Automation System Using YOLOv11 and PLC-Based Actuation
papers.authors: Lara Sobh, Marc Nahhas, Francisco Katach El Halabi, Michel Owayjan, Fadi Elias Sleiman
papers.abstract: This paper presents DeltaVisionX, a low-cost industrial automation system that integrates real-time computer vision with PLC-based actuation for object classification and sorting. The system uses the YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once) deep learning model to detect objects on an operating conveyor belt and communicates detection results to a Delta DVP-SE PLC, which actuates pneumatic pistons for sorting. A custom dataset was created, labeled, and augmented to train the YOLOv11 model, achieving a mean average precision of 0.97 with real-time inference of 100 ms per frame. Encoder-based tracking ensures reliable synchronization between detection and actuation, supporting a throughput of 80 objects per minute. Results show that affordable, locally developed automation can reduce labor dependency and improve manufacturing efficiency. The novelty of the proposed system lies in its encodersynchronized vision-PLC integration rather than in the detection model itself. Future work includes integrating a highspeed Delta robot with EtherCAT-based servo control for advanced pick-and-place operations.
